analysis.one_liner: Stops new tax-advantaged retirement contributions for people whose accounts already hold $10 million.
analysis.headline: A senior House Democrat introduced the bill on July 21, 2026 with zero cosponsors; it was sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: People earning above roughly $400,000 a year would be barred from making new contributions to IRAs, 401(k)s, and similar accounts once their combined retirement balances top $10 million, with an excise tax on contributions above that line. Starting in 2034, taxpayers with balances over $10 million would also have to withdraw larger amounts each year, with rules designed to reach money parked in Roth accounts that has never been taxed. The bill does not say what would be done with the revenue it raises.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiary is the broader taxpaying public: the very wealthiest savers would lose part of an unlimited tax shelter, enlarging the tax base. Millions of taxpayers with normal-sized retirement accounts would be untouched, since the thresholds start at $10 million in balances and roughly $400,000 in income.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers, via a broader tax base

how_it_helps.text: No new contributions would be allowed to any retirement plan once a high-income taxpayer's combined balance exceeds $10 million, and excess contributions would face an excise tax.

Starting in 2034, taxpayers over the $10 million threshold would face increased required minimum withdrawals, computed so that half of the amount above $10 million must come out each year — including Roth money that has never been taxed.

The forced withdrawals would be exempt from the 10 percent early-distribution penalty and subject to 37 percent withholding, and affected employees would gain a right to withdraw the excess from their employer plans on demand.
The income thresholds ($400,000 single, $450,000 joint, $225,000 married-filing-separately) and the $10 million balance cap would adjust with inflation after 2027.
Rollovers, inherited accounts, and divorce transfers would not count as new contributions, so the limit targets new tax-advantaged saving rather than money already in the system.

analysis.who_pays: High-income taxpayers — roughly $400,000+ in income — whose combined retirement balances exceed $10 million. They would lose the ability to keep sheltering new savings and, later, would have to pull large sums out of accounts and pay income tax on the pre-tax portion years ahead of schedule.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not direct the revenue it raises to any purpose, so it is a bare base-broadening measure rather than a funded policy.
It reaches only a very small group of taxpayers, so the revenue would be modest relative to the complexity it adds to the tax code.
Critics of forced distributions argue they could force sales of hard-to-sell assets at bad times; the bill itself acknowledges this by carving out illiquid employee stock ownership plan holdings.

Defenders of large retirement balances argue the accounts were built with after-tax or lawfully sheltered money and that retroactively shrinking the tax treatment of savings undermines retirement planning; the bill's ten-year delay for the distribution rules (2034) partly responds to that objection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy aim — ending unlimited tax-sheltered compounding for the richest savers — is a sound base-broadening step that touches almost no one below the top 1 percent, and the bill's transition rules (penalty-free withdrawals, delayed Roth rules, rollover and inheritance carve-outs) show it was drafted to avoid unfairness. The main honest criticism is that it is a statement bill: no revenue purpose, no cosponsors, and reach limited to a few thousand households, so its practical fiscal effect is small.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee in July 2026 and has sat there since, with no hearing, markup, or floor action and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA), the lead Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on July 21, 2026.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has taken no further action on it.
No other member of the House has signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill would take effect for contributions in 2027 and for the larger required distributions in 2034.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income taxpayers with very large retirement accounts are better off, because the limits on their contributions and required withdrawals have not been enacted; the Ways and Means majority has simply not acted on it.

for.name: Rep. Richard E. Neal
for.role: U.S. Representative (MA-1); ranking Democrat on Ways and Means
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill has sat unreferred-to-action since its July 2026 arrival.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no member has opposed it on the record; the only visible partisan fact is that a senior Democrat introduced it and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Financial services (brokerages, mutual fund companies, retirement plan administrators)
industries.note: The bill would stop new tax-advantaged contributions into accounts once a client's balances pass $10 million and force large annual withdrawals later, trimming a small pool of fee-generating mega-accounts. Most assets would remain invested after withdrawal, so the hit to the industry is modest.
These taxpayers would lose part of an unlimited tax shelter: no new sheltered contributions above $10 million, and from 2034 large mandatory withdrawals that trigger income tax ahead of schedule.

analysis.trajectory: A tax bill with no cosponsors, referred to the Ways and Means Committee in late July of an election-year second session, almost never reaches the floor. Unless it attracts cosponsors or is folded into a broader tax package, it will expire when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
